title: Likelihoods, estimates and BIC by hand
promptMarkdown:
Work by hand and show each step. Give probabilities as decimals with a leading zero, to at least three places. The models are those of the lesson: biased responding with parameter $b$; noisy win-stay lose-shift with parameter $\varepsilon$; and Rescorla-Wagner learning with softmax choice, with parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$, values starting at $Q_0=Q_1=0.5$ and only the chosen arm updated.

1. A participant makes $T=201$ choices. On the $n=200$ trials that have a previous trial, $c=170$ choices follow the win-stay lose-shift rule. Write the session's log-likelihood under noisy win-stay lose-shift as a function of $\varepsilon$, derive the maximum-likelihood estimate in terms of $n$ and $c$ (including the case $c<n/2$), and evaluate it.
2. A Rescorla-Wagner learner with $\alpha=0.5$ chooses arm 1 on trials 1, 2 and 3 and receives rewards 1, 0 and 1. Give $Q_1$ after each trial, and $Q_0$ after trial 3.
3. With $\beta=4$, compute the probability that this learner chooses arm 1 on trial 4.
4. Fitted to one session of $T=200$ trials, Rescorla-Wagner reaches a minimised negative log-likelihood of $120.5$ and win-stay lose-shift one of $124.0$. Compute both BIC values with $\mathrm{BIC}=2\,\mathrm{NLL}+k\ln T$, and say which model BIC prefers.
5. In two or three sentences: what does the difference in part 4 license you to say about this participant, and what would you run before saying more?
hintLadder: Each of the 200 later trials follows the rule with probability $1-\varepsilon/2$ and breaks it with probability $\varepsilon/2$; the first trial contributes $\ln\frac12$ whatever $\varepsilon$ is.
Differentiate $c\ln(1-\varepsilon/2)+(n-c)\ln(\varepsilon/2)$, set it to zero and solve; then ask where the estimate falls when $c<n/2$, given $\varepsilon\in[0,1]$.
Only the chosen arm is updated: $Q\leftarrow Q+\alpha(r-Q)$. Arm 0 is never chosen, so its value never changes.
With two arms the softmax is a logistic function of $\beta(Q_1-Q_0)$, and $\beta$ is the inverse temperature: multiply, do not divide.

criteria.criterion: The log-likelihood is written with the first trial as a constant term; the derivative gives the estimate 2(n − c)/n = 0.30; the boundary case c < n/2 (estimate 1) is stated.

levels.label: partially met
levels.description: Value right, boundary case or derivation missing.

criteria.criterion: Values 0.75, 0.375 and 0.6875 with Q0 unchanged at 0.5, and P(arm 1) = 1/(1 + e^(−0.75)) = 0.6792 with beta as an inverse temperature.

levels.label: partially met
levels.description: Values right, but the probability computed with beta as a temperature.

levels.label: not met
levels.description: Both arms updated, or another wrong update rule.

criteria.criterion: BIC 251.60 for Rescorla-Wagner and 253.30 for win-stay lose-shift; Rescorla-Wagner preferred by 1.70.

levels.label: partially met
levels.description: One value right or the penalty misapplied.

criteria.criterion: The difference is in-sample and small; it ranks prediction of this session after a complexity penalty, not the generating mechanism; model recovery in this design (and validation by simulation or a held-out comparison) is named as the next step.

levels.label: met
levels.description: Caveat and next check both explicit.

checkExamples.label: complete solution
checkExamples.text: Part 1: l(eps) = ln(1/2) + c ln(1 - eps/2) + (n - c) ln(eps/2); setting the derivative to zero gives eps = 2(n - c)/n, so eps = 2*30/200 = 0.3, and if c < n/2 the estimate is 1. Part 2: Q1 becomes 0.75, then 0.375, then 0.6875; Q0 stays 0.5. Part 3: p = 1/(1 + e^(-0.75)) = 0.6792. Part 4: BIC for Rescorla-Wagner is 241 + 2 ln 200 = 251.60 and for win-stay lose-shift 248 + ln 200 = 253.30, so BIC prefers Rescorla-Wagner. Part 5: the difference is in sample and small; model recovery in this design comes first.

checkExamples.label: temperature and penalty mistakes
checkExamples.text: Treating beta as a temperature gives p = 1/(1 + e^(-0.1875/4)) = 0.5117. Without the penalty the two BIC values are 241 and 248. The estimate of eps is 0.15.

checkExamples.label: both arms updated
checkExamples.text: Updating both arms gives Q0 = Q1 = 0.6875 after trial 3, so the probability of arm 1 on trial 4 is 0.5.

checkExamples.label: the probability rounded to two places
checkExamples.text: The probability of arm 1 on trial 4 is about 0.68.

difficulty.basis: Hand calculations with stated models: one likelihood derivation with a boundary case, three Rescorla-Wagner updates, one softmax probability and two BIC values, then a two-sentence interpretation.
